verdict.rationale: Keycloak is itself a standards-based OAuth 2.0/OIDC provider. It exposes discovery, token introspection, revocation, device-grant and client-credentials endpoints, and supports dynamic client registration, so a developer can register third-party clients and issue them tokens under their own realm. It does this as a separate server, though, rather than by turning the developer's own application into the provider, and the third-party-facing parts of the flow are thin in the evidence. missing for 10: evidence of embedding the provider in the developer's own app rather than running a standalone server, third-party consent-screen and branded "Sign in with my app" documentation, independent hands-on corroboration of third-party client onboarding.

support.subject: As a developer, I can turn my own application into an OAuth provider that issues tokens to third-party clients ("Sign in with my app")

citations.quote: Keycloak is based on standard protocols and provides support for OpenID Connect, OAuth 2.0, and SAML.
The dynamic client registration endpoint is used to dynamically register clients.
Keycloak exposes a set of endpoints that applications and services can use to authenticate and authorize their users.
The token revocation endpoint is used to revoke tokens. Both refresh tokens and access tokens are supported by this endpoint.
